## Abstract

Stem cells are known to progress through cell cycle during their differentiation. This combination could be necessary for the transcriptional and epigenetic changes directing the conversion of cellular identity. However, the importance of cell cycle progression in this process remains to be formally demonstrated. Here, we address this fundamental question by using human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) differentiation as a model system. We confirm that each cell division upon differentiation results in the acquisition of a new cell identity. Furthermore, cell fate induction occurs before division while mitosis marks commitment. However, blocking cell cycle progression does not alter identity conversion even at the epigenetic level. On the other hand, CDK1 inhibition affects the processing of specific transcripts thereby preventing differentiation. Thus, cell cycle regulators but not cell cycle progression are necessary for differentiation. These mechanisms are likely to be essential for diversity of process occurring during development and in disease.   

## Introduction

 Most mammalian stem cells progress through their cell cycle upon differentiation to generate two (symmetric division) or one (asymmetric division) daughter cells with a new cellular identity. Those include HSCs, NSCs, intestinal stem cells, pluripotent stem cells in vitro and in vivo 1-3. Thus, cell cycle progression could be closely involved in the process converting cell identity in a diversity of stem cells. In agreement, it has been shown that histone modifications, DNA methylation and chromatin organization are linked with DNA replication and cell division4. Thus, epigenetic modification necessary to change cellular identity during differentiation could be initiated in the S phase of the cell cycle allowing the establishment of new epigenetic state after division during differentiation. As a result, cell fate transition occurring during stem cell differentiation could be intrinsically dependent on their cell cycle progression. Answering this fundamental question is crucial to understand the mechanisms by which organs grow or regenerate in a controlled manner. Furthermore, misregulation of proliferation and differentiation is likely to play a key role in malignant transformation. However, studying these mechanisms remain challenging. Indeed, cell cycle inhibition using small molecule or genetic knock out of cell cycle regulators is either toxic or ineffective in vivo. Furthermore, only few model systems allow the differentiation of homogeneous population of cells in controlled and well-defined conditions. To address these limitations, we have developed a culture system allowing the differentiation of hPSCs synchronized for their cell cycle into a near homogenous population of endoderm in defined culture conditions. This approach enables to define precisely the temporality of cell fate decisions and commitment during cell cycle progression upon differentiation. It also allows to study the molecular function of key regulators in specific phase of the cell cycle.  Here we take advantage of this system to determine the importance of cell cycle progression and regulators in differentiation.


## Cell division marks cell identity conversion during differentiation.

To first confirm that hPSCs progress through cell cycle during their differentiation, we conducted live imaging of cells expressing the H2B-Venus reporter gene (hESCs-H2Bv) and undergoing definitive endoderm (DE) differentiation 5. Our protocol allows rapid (48-72h, Fig.1a) and homogenous (> 90% Sox17+/CXCR4+ cells after 72hrs, Fig.1b) production of endoderm cells while following a natural path of development marked by an intermediate mesendoderm stage (ME, TBXT+/MIXL1+/EOMES+)6. Image analyses (See Methods for details) confirm that the time lapse process did not affect the expression of key markers such as SOX2 in hPSCs, TBXT (BRACHYURY) in ME, or SOX17 in DE cells (Fig.1e-g). In addition, mapping the history of individual cells reveal that hPSCs complete two divisions to become DE cells (Fig.1c,d). The first division takes place on average 20h after the induction of differentiation which is significantly slower than the division time of hESCs (15.85 h vs 19.96 h; p < 0.0001, One-way ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparisons test) (Fig.1c, Extended Data-Video). Of note, the lengthening of the first cell division was consistent across cell lines (H9 vs FSPS13B) (Fig. 1c,d, Extended Data Fig.1d,g). On the other hand, the second cell division during differentiation is considerably faster than the first one, with an average division time of ~14h (19.96 h vs 13.94 h; p < 0.0001, One-way ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparisons test). These observations uphold previous studies in the mouse embryo showing cell cycle acceleration in the primitive streak during mesendoderm differentiation and suggest that each cell division might corresponds to different dynamic regulations. These analyses also revealed that cells generated after the first division acquire the expression of ME marker (TBXT, Fig.1f) while daughter cells generated after the second cell division expressed DE marker (SOX17, Fig.1g). Thus, each cell division occurring upon differentiation result in a different cell type thereby confirming cell cycle progression is tightly associated with identity conversion during hPSCs differentiation.

## Induction of differentiation occurs before cell division which marks cell fate commitment.

We then decided to define at which phase of the cell cycle induction of differentiation and cell fate commitment occur. Of note, conventional culture condition contains hPSCs in different phase of their cell cycle (Extended Data Fig.1b) and this heterogeneity7 precludes investigations in the context of cell cycle progression. To bypass this limitation, we developed a method to differentiate hPSCs synchronized for their cell cycle (Fig.2a and Methods). hESCs were first synchronized in G2/M using Nocodazole 8,9 and then allowed to resume their cell cycle while being grown in culture conditions inducing differentiation or maintaining pluripotency (Extended Data Fig.1b,c). Cell cycle analyses show that the resulting cells remain synchronized until the first division (24hr). Importantly, this method does not alter the length or number of cells cycles underwent by hESCs and hiPSCs during DE differentiation (Extended Data Fig.1c,d,g) thereby confirming the suitability of this system. We next took advantage of our culture system to examine the precise time of induction of key developmental regulators during each cell cycle leading to DE. These analyses revealed that the induction of TBXT, MIXL1, and EOMES occurs during the first S phase after induction of differentiation while SOX2 protein starts to decline (Fig.2b,c and Extended Data Fig.1h). Of note, differentiating cells continued to express OCT4/NANOG but not SOX2 after the first division (Fig.2b,c, Extended Data Fig.1c,d,g,h) when TBXT/MIXL1 reach their maximum level (Fig.2b.c and Extended Data Fig. 2h). These observations imply the induction of differentiation is an early event occurring before cell division. Of note, the second cell cycle was marked by a similar pattern in gene expression with the induction of DE markers (SOX17) occurring before the second division with the decrease in ME and remaining pluripotency markers (Fig.2b,c and Extended Data Fig.1c,d,g,h). We then decided to use the same approach to identify the phase during which cell fate commitment (defined as the moment when hPSCs exit pluripotency and lose the capacity to differentiate into ectoderm) happens. For that, synchronized hESCs were differentiated for 12hrs into ME and then transferred back into conditions supporting pluripotency (Fig.2d). The resulting cells recovered normal levels of SOX2 without expressing ME or DE markers (Fig.2d,g,k and Extended Data Fig.1e,i). Similar experiments using culture conditions inducing ectoderm or mesoderm differentiation show that hESCs differentiated for 12hrs toward the endoderm lineages retained the potential to produce alternative germ layers (Fig. 2e,f,h,i,l,m and Extended Data Fig.1f). We then these experiments using cells differentiated for 24hrs and the resulting ME cells were unable to express pluripotency or neuroectoderm markers when grown in culture conditions promoting these cell fates respectively. Nonetheless, these cells maintained the expression of ME markers and the capacity to differentiate into mesoderm or endoderm (Fig.2d,g,k). Thus, the first cell division upon differentiation results in commitment toward the ME lineage. Finally, similar results were obtained with cells grown for 48hrs with the difference that the resulting cells were not able to induce mesoderm markers thereby confirming that the second division marks commitment toward the endoderm lineage (Fig.2d,g,k). Taken together, these findings indicate that cell cycle progression is associated with key events of differentiation including induction of differentiation in S phase and cell fate commitment during division.

## Cell cycle progression is not necessary for cell identity conversion

We then decided to confirm the functional importance of cell cycle progression by performing similar experiments in the presence of the cell cycle inhibitor Hydroxy Urea (HU) or Nocodazole (Noc) for 24hrs (Fig.3a). Synchronized hESCs were differentiated in the presence of these inhibitors and then analyzed for the expression of differentiation and pluripotency markers (Fig.3b). As expected, both drugs impede cell cycle progression in differentiating cells (Fig.3c). However, ME differentiation markers were up-regulated at similar level to control cells (Fig.3d and Extended Data Fig.2a) while SOX2 expression was downregulated. Importantly, these observations were confirmed by RNA-Seq analyses showing that inhibition of cell cycle during differentiation have little impact on the gene expression profile of ME (Fig.3f and Extended Data Fig.2c,e). The only notable difference was the induction of anterior ME after Nocodazole treatment (Extended Data Fig.2f-h) suggesting that cell cycle could interfere with mesendoderm patterning. Taken together, these observations suggest that cell identity conversion independently of the progression of the cell cycle. Concerning cell fate commitment, differentiating hPSCs grown in the presence of inhibitors (E24HU or E24Noc) were transferred into culture conditions promoting pluripotency for 48h (Fig.3h; E24-P, E24HU-P, E24Noc-P). Under these conditions, hESCs were not able to re-expressed SOX2 suggesting that inhibiting cell cycle progression does not block exit from pluripotency (Fig.3i,j). However, cells blocked at different phases of their cell cycle did not respond equally to differentiation conditions. Indeed, HU treated cells show a limited increase in ME expression and pluripotency marker (Fig.3i,j; E24HU-P) while Noc-treated cells maintained low level of specific ME markers (Fig.3i) and acquired MESP1 and FLK1 suggesting the production of cardiac mesoderm (Fig.3j). Thus, inhibition of cell cycle progression could have varying impact on cell fate commitment depending on the phase of the cell cycle affected. Altogether, our findings show that cell cycle progression allows efficient cell fate commitment without being necessary to exit pluripotency or to induce differentiation.

## Cell Division is not Required for the Epigenome Remodeling 

The results described above suggest that transcriptional changes associated with cell identity can occur independently of cell cycle. However, cell identity conversion is also closely associated with epigenetic modifications including histone H3 lysine 4 mono-methylation (H3K4me1) and H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27Ac) 10,11 on cis-regulatory elements such as enhancers 12. Thus, we decided to investigate the importance of cell cycle progression on these modifications by performing ChIP-seq analyses of H3K4me1 and H3K27Ac during endoderm differentiation in the presence or absence of cell cycle inhibitor. We examined the combinatorial interaction of these two histone marks, within their genomic context and among cellular conditions (UD, E24, E24HU, E24Noc) based on the ChromHMM algorithm 13. We identified ten chromatin states (E1-10, fig.3e) which exposed distinctive epigenetic patterns associated to known genomic elements, such as promoters, enhancers, gene bodies, TSS among others (Fig.3e and Extended Data Fig.3c,d). Chromatin states E1, E2, E3, E6, and E9 were particularly dynamic with E2, E3, and E6 concentrated in regions away from the TSS, suggesting that they represent actual enhancers (Fig.3e and Extended Data Fig.3d,g). On the contrary, E1 and E9 were enriched in regions overlapping the TSS, suggesting that they correspond to promoters (Extended Data Fig.3d,g). As expected, the levels of H3K4me1/H3K27Ac at enhancers were highly variable during differentiation (Fig.3e) while the regions close to expressed genes displayed higher levels of H3K27Ac or H3K4me1 than those linked to silenced genes confirming that these chromatin states were linked to transcriptional activity. Accordingly, we found that binding sites for transcription factors (TFBS) involved in sustaining pluripotency or the induction of ME and DE formation were highly enriched in these genomic regions (Fig.3e). Importantly, the average enrichment of the histone modifications at these putative enhancers was strikingly similar regardless of the capacity of the cells to divide during the differentiation (Fig.3e and Extended Data Fig.3f), indicating that cell division is not required for the epigenetic remodeling associated to cell differentiation. Together our results revealed that epigenetic modifications directing cell identity conversion during differentiation can be established without cell division or normal cell cycle progression.

       

## CDK1 enables cell identity conversion by controlling the translation of specific transcripts.  

 Our results appear to contradict previous reports showing that cell cycle machinery have a direct role in differentiation of hPSCs 7. To address this question, we inhibited the activity of CDKs which are the main regulators of cell cycle progression. We observed that decrease in CDK4/6 or CDK2 activity have a limited effect on mesendoderm specification (Fig.4a-c). On the other hand, inhibition of CDK1 during differentiation14 fully blocks the expression of TBXT and EOMES and results in the persistent expression of the SOX2 protein (Fig.4c). Intriguingly, under these conditions, OCT4 protein was still down-regulated, indicating that the treated cells adopted an alternative cell fate (Fig.4c). Similar results, were obtained by conditional knock-down of CDK1 using inducible shRNA expression (Extended Data Fig.4a,c). To further validated these observations, we decided to perform RNA-seq on differentiated cells after CDK1 inhibition or knock down. To our surprise, these analyses showed that the levels of transcripts coding for key regulators of mesendoderm formation (TBXT, MIXL1, EOMES) were still induced in cells lacking CDK1 activity (Fig.4d and Extended Data Fig.4f). These results were corroborated by qPCR (UD vs E24, UD vs E8-24RO, Supplementary Table 1 and 2; UD vs. E24woTET, UD vs. E24TET, Supplementary Table 3-5; n=3, One-way ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, padj≤0.0001). This observation indicates that CDK1 activity is necessary for the induction of ME markers at the protein level but not at the transcriptional level. Interestingly, CDK1 has been shown to controls protein synthesis in cancer cell line by activating the RNMT-dependent deposition of 7-methylguanosine on RNAs (m7G) during the G2/M transition 15. Hence, we wondered whether CDK1 could fulfil a similar function during hPSCs differentiation. To validate this hypothesis, we first used proximity ligation assays (PLA) 16 to demonstrate that CDK1 interacts with RNMT in undifferentiated cells and that this interaction increased during ME differentiation (Extended Data Fig.5a). Furthermore, immunoprecipitation of methylated RNA assays (meRIP) showed the depletion of CDK1 activity reduces the levels of m7G on TBXT and EOMES transcripts while having no effect on SOX2 and OCT4 (Extended Data Fig.5b). This finding suggested that the CDK1-regulated m7G-deposition is limited to a subset of genes involved in ME formation. These results were confirmed at the genome wide level using meRIP sequencing (meRIP-seq) (TBXT, EOMES and SOX2, Fig.4e and Extended Data Fig.6a,b). Interestingly, differential methylation analysis indicated that an average of 32% of the transcripts carrying 7mG are affected when CDK1 function is depleted (n=1765 differentially methylated transcripts in E24 vs E24RO, n=1781 differentially methylated transcripts in E24woTET vs E24TET (Fig.4e,f and Extended Data Fig.6c-g, peak cut-off FDR=0.05). Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed that the genes most widely affected by the depletion of CDK1 activity during ME formation are involved in RNA processing, cell cycle, regulation of chromatin, epithelium morphogenesis and also primary neural tube formation (Extended Data Fig.6h). Overall, these results indicate that CDK1 control the methylation status of a diversity of transcripts during cell cycle progression upon differentiation. This activity allows the translation of key genes involved in ME formation just during cells division thereby providing an essential step for the process converting cell identity. 

## Discussion.

Added together our results reveal the temporality by which cell identity conversion occur during differentiation. It starts during the G1 phase when cells receive inductive signal of differentiation17 and continue in S with the induction of transcripts coding for key markers of differentiation. However, cell fate commitment is locked only after division while cell cycle regulators especially CDK1 allow the production of developmental regulators protein just after G2/M. This model suggests that stem cells start to change of identity before their first division and thus that initiation of differentiation could be controlled by factors produced in few hours after the induction of differentiation in the G1 phase. However, this hypothesis is unlikely since RNA-Seq analyses have so far failed to identify such factors (Pedro Madrigal, data not shown). Thus, differentiation could result from the re-organisation of existing transcriptional networks by signalling of differentiation. This hypothesis could explain why normal cell cycle progression is not required to change cellular identity. Indeed, simple reorganisation of transcriptional network could act more effectively to “prime” the cells before division independently of new transcriptional event in S phase or mitosis. Nonetheless, this model also implies as confirmed by our genome wide analyses that major epigenetic changes can occur without cell cycle progression. Of note, we can’t exclude that additional epigenetic marks could rely on cell cycle progression. Indeed, proper cell fate commitment seems to be in part dependent on cell cycle suggesting that specific phases of the cell cycle could be necessary to establish the appropriate epigenetic state restricting capacity of differentiation. More broadly and considered in the context of development, our results could infer that proliferation is primarily require for morphogenic movement or for producing the right quantity of cells without being necessary for cell fate decision. However, our results also uncovered more complex interplays involving cell cycle regulators. Indeed, CDK1 seems to be necessary to coordinate transcription and translation during cell cycle progression upon differentiation. Moreover, previous studies have shown that CDK4/6 directs the activity of signalling pathway and transcription factors to define the propensity of differentiation hPSCs. Interestingly, CDKs and other cell cycle regulators such as Cyclin D and Rb proteins have been shown to be necessary for differentiation of neuronal stem cells and hematopoietic stem cells thereby suggesting that cell cycle regulators could be necessary to coordinate molecular mechanisms directing cell identity conversion during differentiation of a diversity of stem cells. Thus, these factors could have independent function in cell cycle progression and differentiation. To conclude, our results reveal novel mechanism coordinating cell cycle progression, protein synthesis, and cell identity conversion. Ultimately, these mechanisms are likely to be essential for diversity of process occurring not only during development or tissue repair but also in disease.   

## RNA-Seq analyses comments:

The results described above have major implications for epigenetic regulation occurring during differentiation. Indeed, S phase and G2/M have been proposed to confirm our findings, we generated global gene expression profiles by RNA-seq. Calculation of the Euclidean distances showed a strong similarity between biological replicates and clear separation of the UD vs. ME samples, regardless of their capacity to divide (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Differential gene expression was calculated for each combination of UD vs. ME cells (UDvsE24, UDvsE24HU, or UDvsE24Noc, p-adj ≤ 0.01, FDR 1%, |log2FC ≥ 2|, See Extended methods for details), which resulted in a total of 1412 differentially expressed genes (Extended Data Fig. 2C).  Out of these, 513 genes were up and 898 genes down-regulated (UD vs. ME, Extended Data Fig. 2C). K-means clustering revealed 6 well-separated groups, with clusters 1 and 2 being the most prominent ones (1: 244 up-regulated genes, 2: 617 down-regulated genes, Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 2f). Functional classification analysis through gene ontology (GO) confirmed the ME identity of the differentiated cells, with TBXT, MIXL1, NODAL, MSX2, and WNT3A being among the genes with the highest levels of expression in cluster 1. Cluster 2, on the other hand, concentrates genes such as SOX2, TBX1, FOXJ1, SIX3, PBX1, KCNN2, CAMKV, and EMX1, confirming that the ME cells were in the process of shutting down the pluripotency and neuro-ectoderm programs (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Although the majority of the differentially expressed genes (861 genes) were regulated similarly, regardless of the capacity of the cells to divide during differentiation, there was a limited cohort of genes that displayed a distinctive pattern depending on whether the cells were blocked in the S or G2/M phase during differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 2f,h). For instance, cluster 3 showed 150 genes strongly up-regulated in UD vs. E24 and UD vs. E24Noc, but a weak or no up-regulation in UD vs. E24HU; on the other hand, cluster 4 displayed 112 genes up-regulated in UD vs. E24 and UD vs. E24HU, but no up-regulation in UD vs. E24Noc. Importantly, these cell cycle–related expression patterns were not exclusive of the up-regulated genes. Cluster 5 presented 104 down-regulated genes in UD vs. E24 and UD vs. E24HU, but only a weak down-regulation in UD vs. E24Noc; and cluster 6 displayed 183 down-regulated genes in UD vs. E24 and UD vs. E24Noc, but a weak or no down-regulation in UD vs. E24HU (Extended Data Fig. 2f). To verify that this segregation was significant, we calculated differential expression among the ME samples (E24 vs. E24HU or E24 vs. E24Noc). This analysis revealed that only a few genes passed our significance differential expression threshold (p-adj ≤ 0.01, FDR 1%, |log2FC ≥ 2|, Extended Data Fig. 2e), indicating that most of the genes in these groups are indeed regulated in similar ways. Nonetheless, GO analysis indicated that each of these clusters contains genes involved in specific biological functions. Specifically, clusters 3 and 4 concentrate genes related to the induction of divergent developmental pathways: the formation of lateral mesoderm and paraxial mesoderm respectively 18, which is consistent with a slight anteriorization of the ME produced in the presence of nocodazole (E24Noc), as suggested by the expression of a battery of HOX genes (HOXA1, HOXA3, HOXA13, HOXB9, and HOXD1; Extended Data Fig. 2f,g). Overall these results indicate that cell division is not required for cell differentiation, although changes in the time that the cells spend in S or G2/M phase during differentiation may affect the outcome of the differentiation.


## Methods.

hPSC culture. hESCs (H9/WA09 line; WiCell) and hiPSCs (FSPS13B) were grown on Vitronectin VF (Stem Cells Technologies, #07180) and cultured in either commercial E8 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A1517001) or E6 media supplemented with 2 ng/mL transforming growth factor b (R&D) and 25 ng/mL fibroblast growth factor 2 (Dr. Marko Hyvönen, Cambridge University) making complete E8 media as described by Chen et al 19. Cells were fed every day and split every 4-5 days using 0.5 mM EDTA (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

hPSC Synchronization Using Nocodazole. For synchronization into the G2/M phase of the cell cycle, cells were treated with 100 ng/mL of nocodazole (Sigma-Aldrich) for 16 hr. For differentiation following nocodazole treatment, cells were plated and treated with nocodazole 2–3 days after plating. Following two washes with E8 media, cells were induced to differentiate using the protocols described in above.

hPSC differentiation. Differentiation was initiated in adherent hESC cultures 24h after passaging. Definitive endoderm specification was induced in three days (unless stated otherwise) by culturing cells in CDM (with insulin) with 80 ng/ml FGF2, 10 μM LY294002 (PI3K inhibitor; Promega), 100 ng/ml activin-A and 10 ng/ml BMP4 (R&D) and CHIR99021 (Tocris) for the first 24h. On day 2, the cells were cultured in same medium without CHIR99021. On day 3, the cells were transferred to RPMI-B27 media supplemented with 80ng/ml FGF2 and 100ng/ml Activin-A. The cells were incubated for the final 24h in same medium supplemented only with FGF and Activin-A. Mesendoderm (ME) cells correspond to the first day of endoderm differentiation. Mesoderm cells were generated as previously described by Mendjan et al 20. For lateral plate mesoderm (LPM) formation, cells were cultured for 48 hours in CDM-PVA supplemented with 20ng/ml FGF2, 10μM LY294002 (Promega) and 10ng/ml BMP4 (R&D). Neuroectoderm cells were generated as follows: On days 1 and 2 the cells were cultured in CDM-BSA supplemented with 20ng/ml FGF2, 3μM CHIR99021, 0.1μM LDN193189 and 10μM SB431542, changing medium daily. From day 3 to day 4 cells were cultured in Neurobasal medium/DMEM F12 (1:1 ratio) supplemented with N2-B27, 1% glutamine, 10μM SB431542 and 0.7% β-mercaptoethanol, changing medium daily. All differentiations were carried out with cells growing on Vitronectin.

For experiments of cell fate commitment, cells were incubated for 12, 24 or 48 in Endoderm differentiation medium after cell synchronization. At the specified times, cells were washed three times with fresh E6 medium and then incubated with the corresponding medium for 3 more days following the protocols described above. For the experiments involving cell cycle blockage, Hydroxyure (HU, 200 µM) was added at time 0, right after nocodazole removal and at the same time of ME induction. This was required to allow cells to reinitiate the cells cycle, blocking them in the following S-phase. To block cells in the following G2/M phase during ME differentiation, cells were allowed to differentiate normally after nocodazole removal. 12h into the ME lineage, 100 ng/ml of nocodazole was added to the differentiation medium, so that the cells could be block in G2/M phases of the cell cycle. 

Cell Cycle Profile Analysis. Cell cycle profile analysis was performed using the Click-iT EdU Pacific Blue Flow Cytometry Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer's instructions. In summary, cultured cells were incubated at 37°C with 10 μM EdU (5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine) for 1 hr and harvested using cell dissociation buffer (Gibco). After three washes with PBS/1% BSA, cells were fixed with 1% paraformaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature and washed three more times with PBS/1%. Cells were then permeabilized for 15 min with saponin-based permeabilization/wash buffer and incubated with the Click-iT reaction cocktail for 30 min protected from light. Cells were washed once with saponin-based permeabilization/wash buffer and stained for DNA content using the DAPI (Invitrogen). Cells were analyzed using Cyan ADP flow cytometer and FlowJo software. 

Live Imaging. For the determination of length and number of cell cycles taking place in undifferentiated (UD), ME, or DE cells, a hESC line carrying the Histone H2B-Venus reporter was cultured as described above, on plates coated with Vitronectin. Cells were incubated in a Biostation CT (Nikon). Images were captured every 15-20 min. To avoid phototoxicity, cells were not imaged for periods longer than 24h. This means that for endoderm differentiation, cells were image in three steps. Day 1 (0-24h of differentiation), Day 2 (24-48h of differentiation), and day 3 (48-72h of differentiation). Images were obtained from at least 3 different biological replicates. Cells were manually tracked using the TrackMate pluggin21 from the Fiji software22. At least 100 cellular divisions were tracked per conditions. Because of the high rate of cell death observed during endoderm differentiation, we tracked cells backwards manner. This means, from the end of the video to the start. We chose cells that divided near the end of the recording and tracked them back to determine the time of the original division. In this way we avoided tracking cells that died in the middle of the recording. Time of division was calculated as the difference between two consecutive divisions. Statistical significance was assessed by performing One-way ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparisons test (****, p≤0.0001). To confirm the phenotype of the cells tracked, cells were fixed with 1% PFA immediately after capturing of the last image, and subsequently immunostained using specific antibodies for pluripotency (SOX2), ME (TBXT) or DE (SOX17). Immunostained samples were observed under confocal microscope and images were obtained for the same cells capture in the Biostation.

Immunofluorescence (IF). For most of the Ifs cells grown on coverslips coated with Vitronectin with the exception of the cells used to track cell divisions, which were stained directly on the plates. Briefly, cells were fixed with 3.7% PFA for 10 min at room temperature, rinsed three times with PBS, and permeabilized for 20 min at room temperature using PBS-0.25% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich). Then cells were blocked for 30 min at 37˚C with blocking solution (PBS-0.25% Triton X-100 plus BSA 1%).  Primary and Secondary antibodies were diluted in blocking solution and incubated for 1h at 37˚C. Cells were washed three times with PBSA-BSA after each antibody staining. Subsequently, cells were stained with DAPI for 5 min at room temperature (0.1 µg/ml DAPI in PBS-0.1% Triton). Finally, cells were mounted and Imaged the next day using a LSM 700 confocal microscope (Leica). 

Flow cytometry. Single-cell suspensions were prepared by incubation in cell– cell dissociation buffer (CDB; Gibco) for 10 min at 37 °C followed by extensive pipetting. Cells were washed twice with PBS and fixed for 10 min at room temperature with PBS, 3.7% PFA. After three washes with PBS, cells were first permeabilized for 20 min at room temperature with PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100, then blocked for 30 min at room temperature with Permeabilization/Wash buffer (BD Bioscience). Primary and secondary or conjugated antibodies were incubated for 1h at 37˚C. Cells were washed three times with this same buffer after each incubation. Flow cytometry was performed using a Cyan ADP flow cytometer, and at least 10,000 events were recorded. Data analysis was performed using FlowJo X. 

Molecular cloning. Plasmids carrying inducible shRNAs were generated by cloning annealed oligonucleotides into the pAAV-Puro_iKD as previously described by Bertero et al 23.  Multiple shRNA for the CDK1 and CDK2 gene were obtained from either previous publications (CDK124) or from the pool of validated shRNA at the Sigma-Aldrich database (CDK2). A single G (guanine) was added at the 5’ end of the shRNAs not starting with G or A. shRNAs were introduced in the psOPTiKD plasmid between the BglII and SalI-HF sites. The psOPTiKD-shCDK vectors were targeted to the AAVS1 locus by using the following vectors: psOPTiKD-shCDK, pZFN.AAVS1-KKR, and pZFN.AAVS1-ELD; based on the method described by Bertero et al23. Briefly, single cells (H9 cells) were nucleofected using the Lonza P3 Primary Cell 4D-Nucleofector X Kit and the cycle CA-137 on a Lonza 4D-Nucleofector System, on feeder-free conditions. Monoclonal colonies were selected for 7-10 days with 1 μg/ml of Puromacin (Sigma). Unless otherwise described in the results or figure legend sections, tetracycline hydrochloride (Sigma-Aldrich) was used at 1μg/ml to induce the expression of the shRNA. The efficiency of shRNA in reducing the CDK1 protein levels was determined by western blotting. Based on those results, we carried out our experiments using the psOPTiKD-shCDK1.1 construct (shCDK1.1: Top Oligo: GATCCCGCTGTACTTCGTCTTCTAATTCT CGAGAATTAGAAGACGAAGTACAGCTTTTTTG; Bottom Oligo: TCGACAAAAAAGC TGTACTTCGTCTTCTAATTCTCGAGAATTAGAAGACGAAGTACAGCGG) and the psOPTiKD-shCDK2.1 (shCDK2.1: Top Oligo: GATCCCGGCATTCCAATCTATTGCTTC ACCTCGAGGTGAAGCAATAGATTGGAATGTTTTTG; Bottom Oligo: GGCCGTAAGG TTAGATAACGAAGTGGAGCTCCACTTCGTTATCTAACCTTACAAAAACAGCT).

Proximity ligation assay. Proximity ligation assay (PLA) was performed using the Duolink In situ Red Starter Kit Mouse/Rabbit (Sigma-Aldrich). Cells were cultured on glass coverslips and prepared by fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS for 10 min at room temperature, followed by two gentle washes in PBS. All subsequent incubations were performed at room temperature unless otherwise stated. Samples were permeabilized in PBS containing 0.25% Triton X-100 for 20 min, blocked in PBS with 0.5% BSA for 30 min, and incubated with the two primary antibodies of interest (diluted in PBS with 0.5% BSA; mouse anti CDK1 and rabbit anti RNMT) for 1 h at 37 °C in a humid chamber. The Duolink In situ PLA probes (anti-rabbit minus and anti-mouse plus) were mixed and diluted 1:5 in PBS with 0.5% BSA, and pre-incubated for 20 min. Following two washes with PBS containing 0.5% BSA, the coverslips were incubated with the PLA probe solution for 1 h at 37 °C in a humidified chamber. Single-antibody and probes-only negative controls were performed for each antibody tested to confirm assay specificity. Coverslips were washed twice in wash buffer A for 5 min under gentle agitation and incubated with 1× ligation solution supplemented with DNA ligase (1:40 dilution) for 30 min at 37 °C in a humidified chamber. After two more washes in wash buffer A for 2 min with gentle agitation, coverslips were incubated with 1× amplification solution supplemented with DNA polymerase (1:80 dilution) for 1 h 40 min at 37 °C in a humid chamber. Samples were protected from light from this step onwards. Following two washes in wash buffer B for 10 min, the coverslips were dried overnight, and finally mounted on a microscope slide using Duolink In situ Mounting Medium with DAPI. Images of random fields of view were acquired using a LSM 700 confocal microscope (Leica) using a Plan-Apochromat 40×/1.3 Oil DIC M27 objective, performing z-stack with optimal spacing (~0.36 μm). Images were analysed automatically using ImageJ. For this, nuclear (DAPI) and PLA z-stacks were first individually flattened (max intensity projection) and thresholded to remove background noise. 

Chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing library preparation. 5 × 106 cells were fixed in 1% PFA for 10 min. Cells were sonicated and an aliquot of 5 µl of sonicated we used to purified fragmented DNA. This DNA was used to check quality of sonication (Samples with fragment ranging from 200-800 bp were used). 4 ug of chromatin were used for each chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP). ChIP was performed using a previously described protocol9. Following pre-clearing, the lysate was incubated for 3h with the antibodies of interest. Immunoprecipitated complexes were purified using protein G-Dynabeads (Invitrogen), washed three times with low-salt buffer (0.1% SDS, 1% Triton X-100, 2 mM EDTA, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 150 mM NaCl), once with high-salt buffer (0.1% SDS, 1% Triton X-100, 2 mM EDTA, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 500 mM NaCl), once with Tris-EDTA (TE)–NaCl buffer (1 mM EDTA, 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8, 50 mM NaCl). Immunoprecipitated complexes were subsequently reverse cross-linked and RNAse treated overnight at 65˚C in elusion buffer (SDS 1%, 0.1 M NaHCO3). The next day, samples were treated with proteinase K (Promega) at 42˚C for 3h. Finally, ChIPed DNA was purified using QIAquick PCR purification kit (Qiagen) and quantified by qPCR using specific primers. Data was expressed as % of the input. After qPCR validation, ChIP DNA were used to build ChIP-seq libraries for sequencing using NEBNext® Ultra™ II DNA Library Prep Kit from Illumina and sequenced in an Illumina Hiseq4000. Library preparations and sequencing were carried out by the Sequencing Core Facility at the Wellcome Sanger Institute.

ChIP-seq analysis. Base calling was done using illumina package RTA v2.7.7, and instrument control package called HCS v3.4.0.38. Reads were aligned to hg38Patch11 reference genome. Alignment files were converted into BAM files and regions of ChIP enrichment over input (peaks) were identified using MACS (version 2.0) on individual replicates, with the following settings: --broad, --broadCutoff 0.1, --keepDup 1, FDR 0.05, gsize=2913022398, --bw 300, --mfold 5 to 50, for pair-end reads. Only peaks present in both replicates were considered for subsequent analysis. Peaks were annotated to the closest genomic feature by using the annotatePeak function from the ChipeakAnno package25 (Bioconductor). To capture the significant combinatorial interactions between different chromatin marks in their spatial context (chromatin states) we used ChromHMM v.1.1013,26, which is based on a multivariate Hidden Markov Model. Binary files calculated as enrichments over input were subsequently used to compute the fold enrichment and emission parameter models. Bed files containing the segmentation estates were used to plot histone modification profiles using deepTools2.027. Briefly, to generate a sequencing-depth-normalized continuous profiles of read coverages over input, bam files were converted into bigwig files using the bamCompare function from deepTools using the following settings: pseudocount 1 --binSize 10 --normalizeUsing RPKM --effectiveGenomeSize 2913022398 --ignoreDuplicates --samFlagInclude 64. These files were used to calculate matrixes of scores per genome region using the computeMatrix function from deepTools. Genome regions were defined as the chromatin states (bed files) generated by ChromHMM. Then, Heatmaps and summary plots of enrichments over input were generated with the plotHeatmap and plotProfile functions from deepTools. For H3K4me1 and H3K27Ac, we compute matrixes centered at the reference point ± 5Kb for each segmentation group separated based on whether genes were upregulated or downregulated in UD vs ME cells (Cluster 1 or cluster 2, figure 3f). Read coverage correlation and PCA analysis for read coverage of samples were carried out using the functions plotCorrelation and plotPCA respectively, after running multiBigwigSummary, which computes the average scores for each of the files in every genomic region by running the program in bins mode. Binding motifs (TFBS) enriched in each chromatin state were HOMER v4.10. The distribution and distance of the chromatin states identified by the ChromHMM algorithm in relation with the TSS of genes was calculated by the functions plotAnnoBar and plotDistToTSS from the ChIPseeker package from Bioconductor28. Genes were annotated against the UCSC list of Known genes for the hg38 genome version using the ChIPseeker. ChIP-seq tracks for visualization were made using the Gviz package from Bioconductor29.  Replicates were combined for visualization proposes only.

RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing. Poly-A purified opposing-strand-specific mRNA libraries were prepared from 200 ng of total RNA using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA HT sample preparation kit (Illumina). Samples were individually indexed for pooling using a dual-index strategy. Libraries were quantified both with a Qubit (ThermoFisher Scientific) and by qPCR using the NGS Library Quantification Kit (KAPA Biosystems). Libraries were then normalized, and pooled libraries were diluted and denatured for sequencing on the Illumina Hiseq4000 according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 

RNA-seq Analysis. Reads were aligned with HISAT2 aligner (v2.1.0)30 to the hg38.84 reference genome. Aligned reads were counted using the Rsubread package31 and differential expression analysis were carried out with DESeq2 package32, based on protocol described by Michael I. Love, Simon Anders, and Wolfgang Huber (http://bioconductor.org/packages/rele ase/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html; https: //www.bioconductor.org/help/work flows/rnaseqGene/). A combined cut-off of negative binomial test P < 0.01 and abs.FC > 2 was chosen. K means clustering was carried out with all expressed genes using the k means clustering function in base R, after determining the optimal number of clusters with a combination of the elbow, silhoute, and Gap Statistics methods using the factoextra and NbClust R libraries.  The result was used to generate the corresponding heatmap of gene expression using Complex heatmaps package from Bioconductor33. Gene onthology analysis were performed with the GOsummaries package from Bioconductor34. 

Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (meRIP). Approximately 5 × 106 cells were used for each RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) using the RiboCluster Profiler RIP-Assay Kit (MBL) following the manufacture’s recommendations. Briefly, cells were collected as single cells using Cell dissociation Buffer, enzyme free (ThermoScientifics), counted, and immediately processed. Immunoprecipitation reactions were pre-cleared for 1h at 4˚C with 30 μl of protein-G dynabeads, then 10 µl of lysed were saved as pre-immunoprecipitation input and stored at −80 °C for subsequent RNA extraction. The rest of the samples were incubated with 500 µl of 1µg of antibody/protein-G dynabeads for 3h at 4˚C. Antibodies were either anti 7methylguanosine (7mG, mouse, MBL, RN016N) or Normal Mouse IgG (Millipore, 12-371). After immunoprecipitation, the samples were washed and subjected to RNA extraction. From this point, the Input samples were processed in the same way. The resultant RNA was quantified and used for qPCR analysis or the construction of libraries for RNA sequencing. qPCR analyses were carried out in the same was as a regular ChIP experiment. Results were expressed as % of Input.

meRIP sequencing analysis. Methylation enrichment analysis was carried out using the Bioconductor package for R, exomePeak 35. Because this package required single-end reads, paired-end reads were split and only one of the ends was used for the analysis. Reads were aligned with HISAT2 aligner (v2.1.0)30 to the hg38.84 reference genome and subsequently processed by exomePeak as follows: Reads with MAPQ < 30 were filtered out. 7mG peak calling and differential RNA methylation in the exome were assessed using individual replicates for each condition, ‘GENE_ANNO_GTF = GRCh38.84, MINIMAL_MAPQ = 30’, and of the remaining parameters as default (PEAK_CUTOFF_FDR=0.05; DIFF_ PEAK_CUTOFF_FDR = 0.05, DIFF_PEAK_METHOD = "rhtest"). Significantly differential peaks conserved between replicates were used in subsequent analyses. These were annotated to the closest genomic feature by using the annotatePeak function from the ChipeakAnno package25 (Bioconductor). Peaks identified by exomePeak were confirmed by using MACS (version 2.0) on individual replicates, with the following settings: --broad, --broadCutoff 0.1, --keepDup 1, FDR 0.05, gsize=2913022398, --bw 300, --mfold 5 to 50, for pair-end reads. Bed files containing the regions of significant enrichment were used to plot 7mG profiles using deepTools2.027. Briefly, to generate a sequencing-depth-normalized continuous profiles of read coverages over input, bam files were converted into bigwig files using the bamCompare function from deepTools2 using the following settings: pseudocount 1 --binSize 10 --normalizeUsing RPKM --effectiveGenomeSize 2913022398, and --skipNonCoveredRegions. These files were used to calculate matrixes of scores per genome region using the computeMatrix function from deepTools2. Then, Heatmaps and summary plots of enrichments over input were generated with the plotHeatmap and plotProfile functions from deepTools2. We computed matrixes centered at the reference point, ranging from 100bp upstream and 4Kb downstream of the center. meRIP-seq tracks for visualization were made using bigwig files of enrichment over input in the Integrative Genomic Viewer (IGV) from the Broad Institute. For visualization purposes, the three biological replicates were combined. Functional profile comparison was done using the enrichGO function of the clusterProfile package36 from Bioconductor. 

Quantitative real-time PCR. Cellular RNA was extracted using the GenElute Mammalian Total RNA Miniprep Kit and the On-Column DNase I Digestion Set (both from Sigma-Aldrich) following the manufacturer’s instructions. 200 ng of RNA was used for complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis using SuperScript II (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA was diluted 30-fold, and 5 μl was used for qPCR with SensiMix SYBR low-ROX (Bioline) and specific primers (See below). Samples were run as technical duplicates in 384-well plates on a QuantoStudio thermocycler (Applied Biosystems), and results were analysed using the delta-delta cycle threshold (ΔΔCt) approach using PBGD as housekeeping gene. The reference sample used as control to calculate the relative gene expression is indicated in each figure or figure legend. All primers were designed using Primer Blast (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/tools/primer-blast/) and were validated to have a qPCR efficiency of 100% ±5% and a single PCR product. 

Western blots. Samples were prepared by adding Laemmli buffer (final concentrations: 30 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 6% glycerol, 2% SDS, 0.02% bromophenol blue and 0.25% β-mercaptoethanol), and were denatured at 95 °C for 5 min. Proteins were loaded and run on 4–12% NuPAGE Bis-Tris Precast Gels (Invitrogen), then transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes by liquid transfer using NuPAGE Transfer buffer (Invitrogen). Membranes were blocked for 1h at room temperature in PBS, 0.05% Tween-20 (PBST) supplemented with 5% non-fat dried milk and incubated overnight at 4 °C. Primary and secondary antibodies were diluted in the same blocking buffer and incubated at room temperature for 1h (See below). Membranes were washed three times after each antibody incubation. Western blots were developed using Pierce ECL2 Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and exposure with X-Ray Super RX Films (Fujifilm). 

Data availability. Nucleotide sequencing data that support the findings of this study have been deposited to GEO with identifiers: GSE130830. Source Data for the graphical representations found in all figures and Extended Data figures are provided in the Supplementary Tables 1-9. Representative videos for cell tracking, including the tracks are available as supplementary information Videos. Additional data is available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
